## What it does

A systematic equity strategy built on moving-average crossover signals, wrapped in a volatility-regime overlay that scales position size down when realized vol crosses a configurable threshold. The point isn't the strategy itself — naive MA crossovers are well-known to underperform buy-and-hold in most regimes — but to build a clean, instrumented baseline I can iterate against and stress-test future systematic ideas with.

## Why I built it

I wanted a defensible answer to: *when do simple trend-following signals actually outperform buy-and-hold after costs, and which failure modes can a minimal overlay fix?* Reading papers gives you the headline; building it yourself shows you the texture — turnover, slippage assumptions, regime transitions, calendar effects. Those textures are where most "obvious" strategies die.

## What I built

- **Data layer:** daily OHLCV for a 50-stock US large-cap universe, pulled from [TBD: data source — likely Polygon, EOD Historical, or yfinance]
- **Signal layer:** configurable fast/slow moving-average windows; entries on bullish crossover, exits on bearish crossover or stop
- **Risk overlay:** rolling realized-volatility regime detection; position sizing decays linearly above a threshold
- **Cost model:** explicit transaction costs and slippage; tax drag is flagged but not modeled
- **Execution layer:** vectorized backtest with daily rebalancing; designed so the same code can drive paper trading

## Key design choices

- **Single-asset evaluation first, then portfolio.** Many MA strategies that look fine in aggregate fall apart on individual names. I wanted to see the per-ticker distribution before claiming anything.
- **Linear vol-scaling, not binary.** A binary on/off switch over-trades the regime transition. Linear scaling smooths the handoff and is easier to debug.
- **Transaction costs as a first-class parameter.** Most academic backtests assume zero costs. I treated this as the strategy-killer it actually is.
